prospective cohort study or registry • Evidence from a well-conducted meta-analysis of cohort studies Supportive evidence from a well-conducted case-control study C Supportive evidence from poorly controlled or uncontrolled studies, including: • Evidence from randomized clinical trials with one or more major or three or more minor methodological flaws that could invalidate the results • Evidence from observational studies with high potential for bias (such as case series with comparison with historical controls) • Evidence from case series or case reports Conflicting evidence with the weight of evidence supporting the recommendation E Expert consensus or clinical experience Of course, published evidence is only one component of clinical decision-making

. Clinicians care for people, not populations; guidelines must always be interpreted with the individual person in mind. Individual circumstances, such as comorbid and coex- isting diseases, age, education, disability, and, above all, the values and preferences of the person with diabetes, must be con - sidered and may lead to different treat- ment goals and strategies. Furthermore, conventional evidence hierarchies, such as the one adapted by the ADA, may miss nu- ances important in diabetes care. For exam- ple, although there is excellent evidence from clinical trials supporting the impor - tance of achieving multiple risk factor con- trol, the optimal way to achieve this result is less clear. It is difficult to assess each com- ponent of such a complex intervention

. It is difficult to assess each com- ponent of such a complex intervention. Evidence to Recommendations All accumulated evidence was reviewed and discussed by all PPC members and sub - ject matter experts during multiple virtual meetings and a 2-day in-person meeting in Arlington, Virginia, in July 2025. Standards of Care recommendations were updated based on the newly acquired evidence, and each recommendation was voted on by the PPC, with 80% consensus requir ed for any recommendation to be approved. . Consensus Report An ADA consensus report is a document on a particular topic that is authored by a technical ex pert panel under the auspices of ADA. The document does not reflect the official ADA position but r ather r epre - sents the panel’ s collective analysis, evalu - ation, and expert opinion. The primary objective of a consensus r eport is to pro - vide clarity and insight on a medical or sci - entific matt er relat ed to diabete s f or which the evidence is contra dictory , emerging, or incomplete. The re port also aims to high - light evidence g aps and to pro pose aven ues f or future resear ch. Consensus reports undergo a f ormal re view pr ocess, in - cluding ext ernal peer review and re - view by the ADA PPC and ADA scientific team, f or publication

. Consensus reports undergo a f ormal re view pr ocess, in - cluding ext ernal peer review and re - view by the ADA PPC and ADA scientific team, f or publication. When participating in a joint consen - sus r eport, ADA, in collabor ation with the partner org aniza tion, designates rep - resent atives who will be involved in all phases of consensus report development (i.e., fr om initiation through publication). Similar to an ADA consensus report, the joint consensus report is intended to highlight an emergi ng area in diabet es care, f ollows the same rigorous review procedur es, and does not reflect the offi - cial ADA position. Scientific Review A scientific r eview is a balanced s yst em - atic review and analysis of lit eratur e on a scientific or medical topic r elated to dia - betes. . A scientific r eview is not an ADA position and does not contain clinical practice recommendations but is pro - duced under the auspices of the ADA by invit ed ex perts. The scientific r eview may provide a scientific rationale f or clinical practice recommendations in the Sta ndards of Care. The category may also include task f orce and e xpert committ ee reports. The endorse ment indicates that the content is scientifically accurat e, rel evant, and valu - able to health car e prof essionals caring f or people with diabetes. While endorse ment conveys support f or the scientific concepts, it may not ext end to every specific st ate - ment or phr asing. Although ADA r epresen - t atives ar e general ly in volved thr oughout the development of these documents, ADA endor sement does not reflect the of - ficial ADA position. content: vi Executive summary The World Health Organization (WHO) convened a technical consultation on 27 –29 August 2024 in Geneva to update the WHO public health research agenda for influenza. Building on the 2009 Agenda, the 2017 update, and multiple 2024 expert consultations, the meeting reviewed progress and set new priorities to address critical knowledge gaps and strengthen preparedness for seaso nal, zoonotic and pandemic influenza. Influenza remains a major global threat, with recurring epidemics and the ongoing risk of potential pandemic viruses emerging from various zoonotic reservoirs. Progress since 2017 includes advances in vaccines, treatments, surveillance and preparedness planning, alongside valuable lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic on viral transmission and public health measures. Yet significant gaps persist. During the consultation, experts refined the Agenda 1 across six streams

content: . Yet significant gaps persist. During the consultation, experts refined the Agenda 1 across six streams. For Stream 1, participants highlighted the urgent need to reinforce surveillance and early warning systems to detect zoonotic viruses with pandemic potential. In Stream 2, they stressed evaluating and optimizing public health and social measures to limit spread, drawing heavily on COVID-19 lessons. Stream 3 emphasized the needs for reducing the disease burden through better vaccine availability, efficacy and delivery, especially in low - and middle -income countries, and accelerating research on next -generation platforms such as messenger ribonucleic acid vaccines. For Stream 4, priorities focused on advancing treatment through new antivirals, monoclonal antibodies and improved clinical management strategies

content: . For Stream 4, priorities focused on advancing treatment through new antivirals, monoclonal antibodies and improved clinical management strategies. Stream 5 underlined the potential of modern tools , including genomic sequencing, artificial intelligence and modelling, to enhance surveillance and better inform decision -makers. Finally, the new Stream 6 focused on improving risk communication, community engagement and infodemic management to counter misinformation and maintain public trust. Equity and the alignment of research with public health policy emerged as cross -cutting priorities to ensure scientific advances benefit all populations. The updated Agenda will guide future research to improve preparedness, reduce transmission, strengthen treatment, and protect communities worldwide. Next steps include embedding these priorities into global health initiatives and mobilizing resources to drive innovation and collaboration

content: 1 Background Influenza remains a major global public health threat, with its full impact on populations still not fully understood. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic exposed major gaps in knowledge and response, prompting the World Health Organization ( WHO) to convene its first global consultation on the public health research agenda for influenza in 2009. This was updated in 2017 to reflect new scientific advances and challenges, aiming to reduce the burden of seasonal influenza and mitigate pandemic risk. The COVID-19 pandemic, though caused by a different virus, provided critical lessons on transmission, public health and social measures, and pandemic preparedness, highlighting the need to reassess influenza research priorities. Recent findings, such as ne w mammalian hosts for avian influenza (e.g. dairy cattle), and advances in vaccine platforms, further underscore the urgency of updating the Agenda

content: . Recent findings, such as ne w mammalian hosts for avian influenza (e.g. dairy cattle), and advances in vaccine platforms, further underscore the urgency of updating the Agenda. In this context, WHO convened a technical consultation in 2024 to refine priorities and ensure the Agenda addresses both persistent and emerging challenges, structured around five streams of work: • Stream 1. Reducing the risk of emergence of pandemic influenza; • Stream 2. Limiting the spread of pandemic, zoonotic and seasonal epidemic influenza; • Stream 3. Minimizing the impact of pandemic, zoonotic and seasonal epidemic influenza; • Stream 4. Optimizing the treatment of patients; • Stream 5. Promoting the development and application of new public health tools, incorporating: o Substream 5A. New technologies in public health and mathematical modelling; and o Substream 5B. Social media tools and risk communication

The 2024 update reflects the need for a holistic, multidisciplinary approach that integrates research on viral transmission, vaccines, interventions and modern tools to strengthen the global response to influenza. Scope and objectives Over several months in 2024, global influenza experts in zoonotic emergence, transmission, disease burden and vaccines, patient management, modelling and communication technologies met online to identify priority research needs. Literature reviews were commissioned for each of the five streams of the WHO public health research agenda. At a subsequent three -day meeting at WHO headquarters, stream leads, co -leads, rapporteurs and WHO staff reviewed the findings, revised recommendations, and agreed on prioritization and implementation timelines

content: 2 Opening remarks The session opened with remarks from Wenqing Zhang, Head of the WHO Global Influenza Programme, who stressed the importance of updating the public health research agenda for influenza in light of recent global health challenges. She welcomed participants a nd highlighted the need to build on lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic and recent technological advances. Reviewing the history of the Agenda, last updated in 2010 and 2017, Dr Zhang emphasized the ongoing need to address knowledge gaps and adapt public health strategies. She underlined the value of collaboration between WHO, academia and research institutions to ensure the Agenda addresses cross-cutting issues and aligns with global priorities. Participants were urged to prepare the Agenda for finalization and implementation by the end of 2024, given the global impact of influenza and emerging threats. Stream 1

Reducing the risk of emergence of pandemic influenza Literature reviews summary The literature reviews focused on two themes. First, advances in surveillance systems for zoonotic influenza in animals have improved early detection, but gaps in coverage and data integration remain, particularly in high -risk areas. Second, serological su rveillance in animals and exposed humans provides vital insights into exposure, immunity and at-risk populations, though standardized methods and stronger coordination between sectors are needed

Following these literature reviews, the group agreed to conduct another review to address the transmission pathways of zoonotic influenza viruses and influencing factors Research gaps identified The discussion highlighted four key research areas: • Analysis of surveillance systems: improving and expanding systems to detect emerging zoonotic and pandemic influenza A virus, making them comprehensive, sustainable and transparent. • Understanding virus–host interactions: studying viral, host and environmental factors influencing transmission and pathogenicity across diverse subtypes. • Vaccines for animal populations: developing and improving vaccines to reduce human exposure, differentiating natural infection from vaccination, and harmonizing serological tools. • Innovative vaccine strategies: adapting and evaluating new technologies and methods to enhance vaccine efficacy and reduce zoonotic transmission

Comments and suggestions from participants on progress and outputs of the stream Participants stressed the need for clear thresholds to trigger public health action from zoonotic surveillance data, noting its underuse in guiding influenza control and response. They called for better integration of human and animal surveillance through a One Health approach. The importance of seroprevalence studies was highlighted to link exposure in animals and humans and capture the full impact of influenza. While novel systems are advancing, traditional surveillance and data -sharing remain underutiliz ed, underscoring the need for sustained funding and resources to ensure both established and new technologies function effectively.

content: 3 Stream 2. Limiting the spread of pandemic, zoonotic and seasonal influenza Literature reviews summary Discussions from the literature reviews focused on three themes. First, understanding influenza transmission routes and factors, including inter - and intra -species spread, aerosol and fomite pathways, and possible transmission via contaminated water. Second, evaluating pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical measures in high -risk settings like live poultry markets, such as closures, vaccination and biosecurity, while recognizing economic and social challenges. Third, assessing the role of public health and so cial measures like hand hygiene, masking and isolation, with the “Swiss cheese” model underscoring the added value of layered interventions

Research gaps identified The discussion highlighted three key research areas: • Analysis of person -to-person transmission: understanding how viral load, immune responses, environment and social behaviours, affect spread, with attention to factors like population density and climate. • Assessment of virus spread dynamics: studying circulation in diverse settings, especially resource- limited areas, and clarifying the role of aerosol, fomite and waterborne routes. • Evaluation of public health and social measures: assessing the implementation and effectiveness of measures such as distancing, hygiene, masking and school closures, and improving data to optimize their use

They called for a clear definition of “impact” and recommended validating existing vaccine effectiveness study designs , drawing on COVID-19 experience. The discussion also highlighted the importance of accurate denominators for vaccination coverage, promoting lifelong vaccination strategies, and using operational research and incentives to boost uptake. Finally, creating an enabling policy environment was seen as essential to align operational research with policy priorities and support the updated Agenda. Stream 4

Optimizing the clinical management of patients with influenza Experts from Stream 4 proposed changing the stream title in the 2017 WHO public health research agenda for influenza from “Optimizing the treatment of patients” to “Optimizing the clinical management of patients with influenza” to better reflect the broader scope of the updated Agenda. Literature reviews summary The literature reviews highlighted several critical areas in influenza research. Host proteins and viral components play a key role in replication and immune escape, informing antiviral strategies. Vaccination remains protective for high -risk groups, thoug h immune responses may be reduced by obesity, ageing or immunosuppression. Bacterial coinfections worsen outcomes, with early antibiotic treatment shown to improve prognosis

content: . Bacterial coinfections worsen outcomes, with early antibiotic treatment shown to improve prognosis. Genetic susceptibility varies across populations, and diagnostic tools like polymerase chain reaction improve outcomes when paired with targeted antivirals. Antivirals such as oseltamivir and baloxavir reduce symptoms and hospitalizations, though effectiveness differs by condition. Adjunctive therapies and optimized regimens for hospitalized patients show promise, but more trials are needed, especially in reso urce-limited settings. Overall, ongoing research on diagnostics, treatments and vaccines is essential, with particular focus on high - risk groups and severe cases. Research gaps identified The discussion identified major knowledge gaps and proposed new directions, focusing on targeted research and evidence-based clinical practices. Two key areas were emphasized:

content: 5 • Pathogenesis and clinical severity: more research is needed on immune response mechanisms in severe influenza to identify prognostic markers and improve management. Genetic susceptibility should be explored through population-based studies, and prevention and treatment of secondary bacterial infections remain crucial due to their impact on outcomes. • Diagnostics and treatment: developing rapid point-of-care tests is vital for timely care, particularly in resource -limited settings. Research should optimize antiviral regimens, address treatment barriers, and expand clinical trials. Improving supportive and intensive care practice s and investigating cytokine abnormalities in severe cases are also priorities. Comments and suggestions from participants on progress and outputs of the stream Experts proposed developing new antivirals, supported by clinical trials and modelling studies, and evaluating monoclonal and polyclonal antibodies for prophylaxis and treatment

Participants recommended expanding antiviral research to include monoclonal antibodies , testing over-the-counter drugs during pandemics, and assessing the extended role of supportive therapies for influenza and other respiratory viruses. They also highlighted the importance of understanding why some healthy individuals develop severe disease, focusing on innate immunity and T cell responses. Cost–effectiveness of early antiviral use, prioritization of high -risk populations, and maintaining routine care during pandemics were identified as critical. Finally, adapting treatment strategies for emerging strains like H5N1, addressing antiviral resistance, and managin g viral sepsis were emphasized. Stream 5. New technologies in public health and mathematical modelling In the 2024 update of the Agenda, experts proposed restructuring Stream 5 and creating a new sixth stream dedicated to communication. Stream 5, retitled “Promoting the development and application of modern public health tools”, will focus on next-generation sequencing, emerging technologies, and the use of modelling to inform public health decision-making. Literature reviews summary The literature reviews focused on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning to predict antigenic changes and viral fitness. AI/machine learning models show promise in forecasting dominant strains and vaccine effectiveness but face challenges in capturing strain interactions (crosstalk) and overall viral fitness

AI/machine learning models show promise in forecasting dominant strains and vaccine effectiveness but face challenges in capturing strain interactions (crosstalk) and overall viral fitness. Generative AI offers potential for modelling viral mutations that may increase transmission and severity, informing vaccine design and control strategies, though reliability depends on dataset quality and validation. The review emphasized the need for more advanced models that integrate diverse biological factors to improve prediction accuracy and guide public health interventions.

The importance of standardized sampling and data integration to improve data quality and consistency was emphasized. • Participants discussed the r ole of modelling in public health . Short-term forecasts and scenario projections are vital for understanding the impact of interventions like vaccine coverage. Improvements in strain forecasting models and the integration of non -biological factors into epidemiological models were also identified as priorities. Developing predictive models for assessing the pandemic potential of emerging strains was also highlighted

A gap remains between public expectations and public health capacities during crises. • Infodemic management: misinformation spreads rapidly via social media; tools are needed to monitor and counter it. “Prebunking” is effective, but fact -checking algorithms require improvement

Addressing hesitancy, maintaining trust and incorporating science communication and advocacy can also sustain funder engagement. • Infodemic management: interventions should target platforms and themes prone to misinformation. Longitudinal analyses of social media and retrospective reviews of COVID -19 responses can identify effective approaches. • Novel communication tools: further research is needed to validate AI, chatbots and other technologies that enhance bidirectional communication and combat misinformation, with integration into broader public health planning

Cross-cutting research topics During this session, three research topics were discussed: • Candidate zoonotic vaccines: At the time of the meeting, 22 H5 influenza vaccines are licensed globally, mostly H5N1, typically egg -based, inactivated, adjuvanted and requiring two doses. Whole-virion vaccines show higher immunogenicity, and some induce cross -reactive antibodies. Live attenuated vaccines elicit responses in children, but correlates of protection for H5 remain unconfirmed, relying instead on seasonal vaccine correlates. • Diagnostic testing strategies: Point-of-care tests and decision -analytic models highlighted the “Polymerase chain reaction -Wait” strategy as effective for maximizing quality -adjusted lifedays, particularly in older adults. Improved rapid diagnostics could strengthen surveillance and test-and- isolate measures, though accessibility remains limited in developing countries, requi ring further research on real-world performance

Effective, culturally sensitive communication and addressing message fatigue are essential. Mobility data offered valuable insights during COVID-19 but raised privacy concerns; expanding data-driven approaches to monitor and adapt strategies in real time was recommended. Outcomes of the meeting • A comprehensive literature review and discussion of the progress made since the 2017 update of the WHO public health research agenda for influenza was conducted. • The outputs of the streams were reviewed, and feedback and recommendations for improvement were provided. • The remaining knowledge gaps in influenza research were identified and analysed, and strategies for addressing these challenges were developed. • The first draft of agreed high-priority areas in influenza research was completed
